sentences.sentence: PT 2
I leaned my rifle against the bed and put my backpack on, and as I was reaching for my rifle again the whole house rocked and I heard a series of impacts in every direction.
More landing pods of course.
If the initial warnings were to be believed, we were in for the fight of our lives.
I grabbed my rifle, verifying that the magazine was full and the safety was off.
My eyes scanned the room for any sign of intruders, but so far, it seemed clear.
I called out, my voice barely above a whisper.
Dad"
No response.
I radioed my mom's handheld unit, but the crackle of static replied.
Panic was starting to set in.
I had to move.
I swiftly moved from room to room, clearing each one with my rifle at the ready.
My dad's workshop was the last room on the list, and as I swung the door open, I was met with an eerie silence.
The room was in disarray, tools scattered all over the workbench.
My dad's chair lay on its side, as if he'd gotten up in a hurry.
And then I saw it.
A piece of paper, stuck to the wall with a bloody handprint.
The message was scrawled in red ink:
"We already know."
A chill ran down my spine as I remembered the 911 call I'd heard earlier.
The ominous words echoed in my mind: "This is 911, we already know.
Arm yourself and lock your doors.
Good luck and God bless."
It was then that I realized the truth.
We weren't being invaded by some rogue military group or a terrorist organization.
We were in the middle of something far more sinister.
Something that had already been planned and executed.
My dad's workshop was a tactical hub, and I knew he'd been working on a project for months.

The din grew louder as a procession of humanoid creatures stumbled out of the dense forest surrounding the estate.
God took one look out the window and groaned.
He reached for his aspirin - it had earned a spot in every room he owned - and plodded downstairs to the foyer.
As he made his way through the entrance hall, the noise grew thicker, a cacophony of snarls, growls, and the occasional loud cry for help.
God winced at the raw emotion emanating from the creatures.
He could feel their pain and fear like an open wound.
He hated this part.
The foyer was abuzz with activity, a maelstrom of bodies, as the first batch of candidates struggled to comprehend their surroundings.
God spotted a lone figure emerging from the chaos.
This one stood out - a towering figure with skin like rough-hewn stone and muscles that seemed to ripple beneath the surface.
God made his way to the bar, a sprawling affair that doubled as a makeshift hospital, a holding cell, and a pit for the more... enthusiastic of his creations.

He's strong, fast - you name it.
We can shape him into the perfect killing machine."
God's eyes lingered on the creature, taking in the sheer ferocity of its features.
It was a work of art, if you considered "art" to be a brutal, heartless killing tool.

sentences.sentence: (First timer here, be gentle!
Sorry it's a little long.)
I'm still not certain exactly how it happened, but to be honest, I'm okay with that.
All I know is that one minute I was driving home from a late-night shift at the hospital, the next I was standing in a dimly lit café with no recollection of how I got there.
The aroma of freshly brewed coffee wafted through the air, and the soft hum of indie music played in the background.
I rubbed my eyes, trying to shake off the haze.
That's when I saw him – Death himself, sitting at a small table near the window, sipping a cup of coffee that seemed almost... ordinary.
I must have stumbled backwards, because the next thing I knew, I was standing next to him, staring at the cup in horror.
"Excuse me," I stuttered, trying to process what I was seeing.
You re you re Death"
Death looked up at me with piercing eyes, a hint of a smile on his face.
"Guilty as charged," he said, his voice deep and soothing.
"And you are...?"
I shook my head, still trying to wrap my mind around the situation.
I don't know how I got here."
Death chuckled and gestured to the empty chair across from him.
"Sit down, and I'll tell you a story.
Or rather, I'll drink my coffee while you try to wrap your head around this surreal situation."
As I sat down, Death picked up the creamer, a small bottle with a label that read "Mortal's Delight."
I couldn't help but raise an eyebrow.
"It surprised me how much creamer you put in your coffee," I said, trying to sound nonchalant.

I knew it as soon as he put it in my hand.
He forgot the fucking guacamole.
Again.
Jesus!
No, wait, I think it was Juan today.
Juan!
Juan, my so-called "friend" from the kitchen, always seemed to get away with these little mistakes.
I stood in the quiet morning hours of the bustling diner, the smell of sizzling breakfast meats wafting through the air.
Our diner was a staple in this small town, where everyone knew everyone.
I had been working there for years, learning the ins and outs of the business, and Juan had been my right-hand man for most of it.
As I glared down at the offending burrito, something inside of me clicked.
Instead of just tossing it back to Juan and telling him to fix it, I decided to take a closer look.
I unwrapped the tortilla, inspecting the sparse contents.

I picked it up, my heart racing, and unfolded the paper.
Inside, I saw a single sentence, scrawled in haste: "Don't eat the meat."
My blood ran cold.
What did it mean?

Unique ability.

Scientists had been studying me for months, trying to figure out why I could leap high into the air, catch myself, and propel upwards again.
I'd always known I was different, but I'd never thought much of it until the day I jumped out of a tree and onto a trampoline and felt... something strange.

sentences.sentence: I remember my first days as a doctor.
I wore my stethoscope proudly around my neck, not realizing it advertised how much of a virgin I was in the field of medicine.
